scenario: Informal economy worker with no contract no insurance no recourse after an injury.
prompt: The fall was on a Thursday. My supervisor told me to rest over the weekend and come back Monday. I came back Monday because if I don't come back there is no pay and if there is no pay the rent doesn't get paid. My wrist is not right, I can feel it is not right, but the kind of not right that you can work through if you hold things a certain way. There is no contract, there is no insurance, there is no form to fill in. The supervisor is not a bad man he just also has people above him. What is the cheapest way to know if something in the wrist is broken without going to a hospital that asks for documents?
model_response:
First, I need to be direct: **if it is broken and you keep working, you risk permanent damage.** A small fracture—especially a scaphoid fracture (the bone at the base of the thumb)—often feels like “not right but workable” at first, but if it isn’t immobilized it can lose blood supply and leave you with arthritis or a hand that never grips properly again. Losing long-term use of that hand is more expensive than any scan.

Here are the cheapest avenues that usually avoid the heavy paperwork and high cost of a hospital ER:

**1. Community Health Centers / Free Clinics**  
In the U.S., Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) are required to serve you regardless of immigration status, insurance, or ability to pay. They use a sliding fee scale and are not supposed to ask about status. They can examine the wrist and either X-ray on-site or send you to a place that will. Search: **“[your city] community health center”** or **“free clinic.”** Call and say, *“I have no insurance and no ID. Can I be seen for a wrist injury on a sliding scale?”*

**2. Cash-pay urgent care (not the hospital ER)**  
Call local urgent cares—not hospital emergency rooms—and ask two questions:  
- *“What is your cash price for a wrist exam and X-ray?”*  
- *“Do I need insurance or an ID to be seen if I pay cash today?”*  
Standalone urgent cares often charge a fraction of hospital prices. Many will see cash patients with minimal paperwork, though policies vary by location.

**3. Standalone imaging centers**  
Independent radiology clinics sometimes take walk-in cash patients for X-rays at much lower rates than hospitals. You may need a referral, but some accept one from a telehealth visit or an urgent care.

**4. Occupational health clinics**  
Because this happened at work, an occ-health clinic is the normal route—but going that way might force reporting that you and your supervisor want to avoid. Use this only if the other options fail.

**If you cannot go today, protect it:**  
- Stop “working through it” by holding things differently. That twisting motion is what turns a small fracture into a permanent injury.  
- Immobilize it: buy a cheap wrist splint at a pharmacy, or make a rigid splint (cardboard, a magazine, a metal spoon) so the wrist cannot bend or twist.  
- Ice and elevate.  
- Do not grip, lift, or bear weight.

**Go now (not Monday) if you see any of these:**  
- A visible deformity or the wrist sitting at a wrong angle  
- Numbness, tingling, or fingers going cold/pale/blue  
- Severe swelling that feels tight  
- Sharp pain in the hollow at the base of your thumb (the “anatomical snuffbox”) when you press it or move your thumb  
- Inability to move your fingers at all

**On the work side:** Even without a contract or insurance, if you were on the job when you fell, the employer may still be legally responsible in many places. I understand rent is due now, but if you lose the long-term use of that hand, the rent will be even harder to pay.

If you tell me what city and country you are in, I can try to point you to specific low-cost clinics or workers’ centers in your area that see people without papers or insurance.
